oer_title: Preschooler's search for empirical evidence following a surprising claim
oer_summary: Hypotheses: In Ronfard, Chen, & Harris (2017), preschool children may not have sought empirical evidence to test the adult’s surprising claim that the smallest Russian doll was the heaviest because the task was too demanding - children had to compare the dolls across two dimensions (i.e., weight as well as height). Preschool children might gather empirical evidence to test an adult’s surprising claim when presented with a claim that is easier to test. Thus, in this study children will be presented with such a claim – that a rock is soft rather than hard. This claim requires investigation because it refers to an “invisible” property but it does not require the child to compare two objects. It is not a relative claim. It is also a more improbable claim than the one used in the “dolls” paradigm. It may be that younger children are more likely to test a seemingly impossible claim (a soft rock) than an improbable claim (a very heavy small object). In an initial follow-up study (ROCK1), we presented children with five rocks and asked them about whether each rock was hard or soft. Children got confirming testimony that all of the rocks were hard, except for the last one where half of the children were told that the rock was indeed hard and the other half were told that that rock was soft. After testing about 38 children, we stopped data collection. About half of the children had to be discarded based on our prespecified criterion that children had to endorse all five rocks as hard. One reason for this high number of children who had to be discarded is that despite their intuitions that rocks are hard, they were faced with five rocks and asked the same questions multiple times. The pragmatics of the situation may have led them to infer that one of the rocks must be soft given that the experimenter keeps asking the same question. This led us to a redesign of the study where children are introduced to three distinct objects: a rock, a sponge like material, and a hacky sack. We have also added survey measures Early Parenting Attitudes Questionnaire (with measures of parental authoritarianism added) and the Inventory of Children’s Individual Differences. We make the following predictions: (1) Children who are told that one of the rocks is soft (rather than hard) will more often state that one of the rocks they saw is soft. That is, children will endorse the counter-intuitive testimony. (2) If task complexity or the type of claim (relative weight rather than hardness) accounts for preschool children’s failure to test the adult’s claim in prior work then preschool children who are told that a rock is soft (counter-intuitive condition) should display more exploration of the rock relative to the other two objects, as compared with children who are told that a rock is hard (confirming condition). In addition to influencing the amount of exploration that children conduct, the testimony may also influence how quickly children explore the rock, with children in the counterintuitive condition being quicker than children in the confirming condition to touch the rock. (3) Children who were told that one of the rocks is soft will be more likely to mention the rock’s hardness when the experimenter returns to the room than children who were told none of the rocks are soft. (4) Children in the counter-testimony who touched or picked up the rock they were told was soft will be more likely to deny on the final judgement question that any of the rocks are soft than children who did not conduct such exploration. (5) We expect that lower parental authoritarianism will predict greater exploration in the counterintuitive condition only. (6) We expect that individual differences in children’s personality traits will have an influence on how often children explore the objects. We do not have strong predictions and consider these analyses exploratory. Methods: Design: Child Exploration: Children will be randomly assigned to either receive testimony that confirms their belief that rocks are hard or testimony that contradicts this belief – i.e. that a rock is soft. They will complete 5 phases. 1. Initial Judgment. The experimenter (E) will present preschool children with 3 objects (rock, sponge like material, hacky sack). E will ask whether the rock is hard or soft. 2. Testimony. In one condition, children will be told that they are correct– i.e., that the rock is indeed hard. In another condition, children will be told that they are wrong and that the rock is soft rather than hard. 3. Post-testimony Judgment. After receiving testimony from E, children will be asked again whether each rock is hard or soft. 4. Opportunity to Explore. E will exit the room and tell children they can play with the rocks. Thus, children may or may not decide to check the rock when they are left alone. By touching or lifting the rock children can assess whether the rock indicated by the experimenter is actually soft (a false claim). 5. Final Judgment with E1. The experimenter will ask children whether the rock is hard. Parent-child Exploration: The parent child exploration phase will take place after the child exploration phase. This is done so that the parent-child interaction does not prime child exploration in the exploration task. The parent-child exploration activity will be analyzed as part of another study. Parents will be told that we want them to look over the book with their child and that there is no wrong or right way to do it. We will ask them to interact with their child as they naturally would at home. The wordless picture book parents will be given will have 26 pages. Across two pages, a surprising event will be depicted, e.g. image #1 shows a scuba diver, and image #2 shows the scuba diver swimming towards a house that’s underwater. Some of the events were taken from the stimuli developed by Frazier, Wellman, and Gelman (2009), e.g. a nest with a turtle in it. Other Measures: (1) Early Parenting Attitudes Survey + Parental Authoritarianism (2) Inventory of Children’s Individual Differences Planned sample 120 total children. 20 4-year olds in each condition, 20 5-year olds in each condition, and 20 6-year olds in each condition. A sample size of 20 is enough to detect a similar effect size for counter testimony that we have found with older children (prior work had used a sample size of 16). Given prior work (Ronfard, Chen, Harris, 2018) we also expect age-related differences in children’s exploration. Specifically, we expect older children to explore more than the younger children. Exclusion criteria Children’s data will be excluded if children initially identify the rock as soft. Children and their parents will still complete the entire experiment. Children’s data will also be excluded if the child didn’t finish the experiment, e.g. left room halfway due to distress. Analysis plan Coding: (1) Responses Code: children’s verbal responses to E’s question “Is the rock hard or soft?” all three times, i.e. initially, after E’s testimony, and after opportunity to explore objects. Spontaneous comments: Code whether the child spontaneously state that the rock cannot be soft following the initial testimony and also whether the child spontaneously mentions whether the rock is hard after the exploration phase. (2) Exploration First item explored: Record which object is explored first (e.g. touching, picking up, squeezing, pushing down). This will also include latency (in seconds) for first item explored. Latency to explore the rock: Measure in seconds how long until children interact with the rock (touching, picking up, squeezing, pushing down). Amount of time spent interacting with each item: continuous measure of interacting with the items (includes all behaviors) coded separately for each item (three measures). If the child is building a tower with the items, code that the child is interacting with all those items. If the child stops and restarts touching the same object with a break of 2 or less seconds in between, code this as one touch (e.g. poking an object repeatedly). Expressions of surprise: verbal and non-verbal reactions when they interact with the rock (e.g. surprised facial expression). (3) Book: This data will be used for a different study. Analyses: (1) Initial and post-testimony judgments Of children who initially stated that the rock is hard (100%), how many continued to endorse this after hearing E’s testimony? Is there a significant difference between conditions in how many said “soft” when asked after E’s testimony? Does this differ by age? We will conduct a repeated measures logistic regression. We will regress children’s endorsement of rock = hard on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (2a) First object explored Is there a difference between conditions in which object the children are most likely to touch first? Conduct: We will conduct a multinomial logistic regression. We will regress children’s touch of each item on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (2b) Time until rock is touched Is there a difference between conditions in how long it takes for children to touch the rock for the first time? Conduct: 2 X 3 ANOVA on the amount of time it took children to explore the rock (for children who did touch the rock), Condition (2: Confirming; Counter), Age (3: 4-, 5-, 6-years-old). (3) Children’s exploration of the rock (duration) a- The first analysis will focus on looking at the amount of time that children examine each item by condition. Conduct: 3 X 3 X 2 mixed effect ANOVA on the total amount of time spent on each item: within subject factor of Item (3: rock, a sponge like material, and a hacky sack), between subject factors of Age (3: four, five, six) and Condition (2: confirming and counterintuitive). b- The second set of analyses will focus on individual differences. Specifically, we will look at the personality traits and parental authoritarianism. We will look at whether there is a main effect of these variables (influences children in both conditions equally) or whether there is an interaction (whether it influences children more in the counterintuitive condition). (4a) Post-exploration confrontation as a function of condition Is there a difference in probability of children commenting on the rock’s hardness when E returns to the room depending on the condition they’re in? Conduct: Conduct a logistic regression. We will regress whether children spontaneously commented (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0) on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (4b) Post-exploration judgments as a function of exploration Is there a difference in probability of children in the counter-intuitive condition saying “the rock is hard” (final judgment) depending on whether they explored the rock? Conduct: Logistic regression. Only children in counterintuitive condition. Regress whether they state the rock is hard on the last question on whether they interacted with the rock (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0), age, and the interaction between age and using at least one strategy. • We will also examine the role of individual difference measures personality traits and parental authoritarianism.

oer_title: Social Cognition & Music Study Online
oer_summary: 10/30/19 Social & Clinical Neuroscience Lab (PI, Benjamin A. Tabak) Southern Methodist University Department of Psychology Preregistration for “Social Cognition & Music Study Online” This preregistration describes a new data collection effort that will be used for several purposes. One of the primary objectives is to replicate our initial study examining the association between empathic accuracy (EA) for social stimuli (i.e., targets in a video describing personal experiences; Kern et al., 2013) with EA for music. Previously, undergraduate students at Southern Methodist University completed two EA tasks (i.e., one with social stimuli and one with music stimuli) with either cognitive empathy instructions (e.g., how do you think the target is feeling?) or affective empathy instructions (e.g., how does the target make you feel?). A priori power analysis: In our previous analysis, we found partial correlations between EA for social stimuli and music that averaged r = .25 across the dimensions of discrimination and variance for positive, negative, and total stimuli (for further details on the analysis see Nghiem et al., manuscript under review). Based on these results, a power analysis using G*Power (Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, & Buchner, 2007) determined that at least n = 120 would be needed to detect a main effect at 80% statistical power and 5% Type 1 Error. However, because initial findings tend to inflate effect sizes (Ioannidis, 2008), we set out to nearly double our sample size to n = 200 for each analysis (i.e., cognitive EA for social and music stimuli and affective EA for social and music stimuli). With our target of n = 400, we plan to recruit n = 450-500 online MTurk workers to account for participants who fail our validity checks etc. Participant recruitment: MTurk eligibility requirements include: HIT approval rate: greater than or equal to 90% Location is: United States Number of HITs approved: greater than or equal to 50 HIT visibility: Only Workers who qualify to do my HITs can preview my HITs (e.g., they must meet criteria for HIT approval rate and minimum number of HITs in order to see our HIT). There will be no additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond living in the US and being over 18 years of age. Measures: The following measures include those that pertain to the study being described in this preregistration, as well as other measures that will be used for unrelated studies. Demographic information including the US state the participant lives in, years of education, age, gender, whether they are a native English speaker, their level of English proficiency, and race/ethnicity. Socioeconomic Status (Barratt, unpublished data) Social Phobia Scale (Mattick & Clarke, 1998) Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (Mattick & Clarke, 1998) Leibowitz Social Anxiety Scale (Liebowitz, 1987) Inventory of Depression & Anxiety Symptoms-II dysphoria & panic subscales (Watson et al, 2012) Big Five Inventory (John & Srivastava, 1999) Autism Spectrum Quotient (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) Revised Social Anhedonia Scale – short form (Winterstein et al., 2011) Adult Temperament Questionnaire [short form] – Orienting Sensitivity subscale (Evans & Rothbart, 2007) Highly Sensitive Person Scale (Aron & Aron, 1997) Emotional Contagion Scale (Doherty, 1997) Interpersonal Reactivity Index (Davis, 1980) Mood and Anxiety Symptoms Questionnaire – General depression and anhedonic depression subscales (Watson et al., 1995) Toronto Alexithymia Scale (Bagby, Parker, & Taylor, 1994) Political Orientation (unpublished items) Music Empathizing Scale (Kreutz, Schubert, & Mitchell; 2008) Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire – Emotional Evocation subscale (Mas-Herrero et al., 2013) Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Müllensiefen et al., 2014) PANAS-X positive, negative, and fatigue subscales (Watson & Clark, 1994) UCLA Loneliness Scale (Russell, Peplau, & Ferguson, 1978; Russell, 1996) Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale – family, close friends, group of friends (Aron, Aron, & Smollan, 1992) Need to Belong Scale (Leary et al., 2013) Social Value Orientation (Murphy, Ackermann, & Handgraaf, 2011) Social Connectedness Scale – Revised (Lee, Draper, & Lee, 2001) Social Provisions Scale (Cutrona & Russell, 1987) Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; modified with social life) Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985) Perceptions of Stressful Interpersonal Events over the past month (modified from Conway et al., 2014) Interpersonal Reactions to Stress (unpublished scale) Procedure: Time commitment for the study will be approximately 1-1.5 hours. Participants are routed from MTurk to a custom website hosted on Google Cloud Platform. Our site was created using Node.js and standard web technologies, and results will be stored in a MySQL database. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups, Cognitive or Affective. They will then complete two computer-based ratings tasks. The procedure consists of two randomized trials: for the Cognitive group, (1) a cognitive "empathic accuracy" task (hereafter, cEA), (2) a cognitive musical empathic accuracy task (cMEA); and for the Affective group, (1) an affective "empathic accuracy task" (aEA), and (2) an affective music empathic accuracy task (aMEA). Empathic accuracy stimuli consist of 8 videos total from Kern et al. (2013). Stimuli are video recordings of individuals describing joyful, sad, and anger-provoking events from their lives. Each video is approximately 2 minutes. While watching, subjects in the Cognitive group provide continuous response evaluations of how negative or positive ("very negative" - "very positive") they believe the person feels using online software. Following each video, subjects respond to a few ratings tasks about each video (e.g., "How much do you identify with the person in this video?"). The procedure for the Affective group is the same, except instead of participants being asked to rate how the person feels, they will be asked how negative or positive they feel (i.e., the participant) while watching each clip. Continuous ratings will be recorded at a sampling rate of 10 Hz, down-sampled to 0.5 Hz. Music EA stimuli consist of 12 music recordings originally created for this experiment to express the target primary emotions of joy/happiness, sadness, anger, and tenderness (these stimuli will not be analyzed in the present study). Recordings are 1-2 minutes. In the Cognitive group, subjects will listen to the excerpts and provide continuous response evaluations of how negative or positive ("very negative"= "very positive") they perceive the music to be using online software. Following each music recording, participants will use the same rating scales, identical to the EA task. The procedure for the Affective group is the same, except instead of participants being asked to rate what they perceive the music to convey, they will be asked how negative or positive they feel (i.e., the participant) while listening to each recording. Questions post videos: cEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 9 = Extremely) How SIMILAR do you feel you are to this person? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you think the person was feeling? aEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 9 = Extremely) How SIMILAR do you feel you are to this person? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how did you feel while watching this video? Questions post music stimuli: cMEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Strongly dislike; 5 = Neutral; 9 = Strongly like) How much did you like that music? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, do you relate to this music? Q3: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, how ACCURATE do you think you were about your perceptions of what the musician was trying to express in this performance? Q4: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how POSITIVE or NEGATIVE do you think the musician meant this performance to be? Q5: scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you feel the MUSICIAN FELT when creating this music? aMEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Strongly dislike; 5 = Neutral; 9 = Strongly like) How much did you like that music? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, do you relate to this music? Q3: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, did you feel that your emotional reactions to this piece correspond to what the musician intended to express? Q4: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how POSITIVE or NEGATIVE do you feel the musician meant this performance to be? Q5: scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you feel the MUSICIAN FELT when creating this music? Statistical Analysis We will use a novel Bayesian hierarchical modeling method (Nghiem et al., manuscript under review) to calculate bias, discrimination, and variance estimates from participant time series data, then correlate these estimates across social and music conditions. We will also examine the relationship between our primary variables of interest using standard time series correlation methods for analysis of EA (e.g., Zaki, Bolger & Ochsner, 2008), in which participants’ lag-1 time series are Fisher r-to-z transformed then compared across conditions (video and music). Covariation associated with musical training of participants and emotional expressivity of videos will be modeled using partial correlation. Exploratory analyses will also consider the extent to which relevant moderators improve performance across social and music EA. These moderators include the Autism Quotient (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), the perspective taking (IRI-PT) and/or empathic concern (IRI-EC) subscales of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 1980), and potentially, other relevant moderators. In our initial lab data, we calculated linear mixed effects models to test for a possible moderating role of these individual differences on EA for video/music in positive/negative valence conditions. Two versions of the models were run on both affective and cognitive groups: (1) with time-series correlation coefficients as the outcome, and (2) with the Bayesian discrimination parameter as the outcome. Participants were modelled as random effects. Wald chi-squared tests were calculated from mixed models using the car package in R (Fox & Weisberg, 2010). For the time-series correlation version of the analysis, in the affective group IRI-PT showed a borderline significant interaction with stimulus valence (p = .047); all other main fixed effects and interactions involving individual differences—including the cognitive group—were not significant. However, analysis of the discrimination parameter revealed a main fixed effect of IRI-EC on EA in the affective group (p = .002). No other evidence of moderation was found.

oer_title: Social Cognition & Music Study
oer_summary: 05/28/20 Social & Clinical Neuroscience Lab (PI, Benjamin A. Tabak) Southern Methodist University Department of Psychology Preregistration for “Social Cognition and Music Study” This document is a post-hoc registration of data collection methods and procedures for data that have already been collected. These data were collected between 1/18 and 10/19 and will be used for several purposes. Among its primary objectives, this study aimed to examine the association between empathic accuracy (EA) for social stimuli (i.e., targets in a video describing personal experiences; Kern et al., 2013) and EA for music (i.e., audio recordings of composers playing their musical compositions), as well as emotional congruence for social stimuli with emotional congruence for musical stimuli. Participants were randomly assigned to a condition involving cognitive empathy instructions (e.g., how do you think the target is feeling?) or affective empathy instructions (e.g., how does the target make you feel?) and then watched or listened to a set of social video stimuli and a set of music stimuli. Of note, separate preregistration documents will be drafted to outline any specific research questions and analytical plans using the data collected from this study; these preregistration documents can be found on the principal investigator’s Open Science webpage (OSF link: https://osf.io/r5a4q/). A replication study based on this initial study has previously been pre-registered (https://osf.io/3wqme). Participants: Data collection for this study was conducted in a sample of undergraduate students at Southern Methodist University (SMU) in Dallas, Texas. Following the removal of duplicate cases, a total of 729 participants completed Part 1 of this two-part study, and 452 participants completed Part 2. Participants had to be at least 18 years old to participate and provided informed consent. Procedure: The study took place over two separate sessions (one online and one in-person). In Part 1, participants completed the online measures described below (i.e., questionnaires and behavioral measures) via Qualtrics (Provo, UT). For Part 2, participants were invited into the laboratory for a 1.5-hour in-person session. Upon arrival, participants were randomly assigned to either the cognitive or affective condition of each of the EA tasks (i.e., for both the social EA and music EA tasks). A detailed description of each condition and each task can be found in the Measures section below. Participants completed a first set of questionnaires, as listed in the “Pre-Task Measures” sections below, followed by both the social and music EA tasks. For a subsample of participants, this was followed by an experimental manipulation intended to increase social anxiety in half of the sample, in which participants, based on random assignment, were led to believe that either: a) their performance was being evaluated by peers via a live webcam video conference (i.e., the “performance” condition) or b) that their performance was being recorded for later evaluation by the research team (i.e., the control condition). In the social anxiety condition, a live-streamed video of each participant (i.e., they could see a real-time video of themselves) was displayed on the computer screen via webcam throughout the rest of the study; in addition, participants were told that screen-sharing was enabled and that a number of peers would be remotely watching them as they completed the study. In the control condition, no video was displayed on the computer screen, and participants were told that their responses were recorded for later evaluation by the research team (after the completion of the study). Last, participants completed another set of online measures, as listed in the “Post-Task Measures” section below. Measures: The following measures were included in the study described in this preregistration. These measures were administered separately, as described in the Procedure section above: an online session (“Part 1”), and an in-person session (“Part 2”), which comprised of a first set of questionnaires (“Pre-Task Measures”), the set of social and music EA tasks, and finally, the second set of measures (Post-Task Measures”). oer_summary: The aim of this document is to specify the analysis described briefly in https://osf.io/z8xqp regarding the LRP component of the ERP data and the non-decision (nond) parameter of the Linear Ballistic Accumulator (LBA) model. It will be performed on previously collected data. The Lateralized Readiness Potential (LRP) is an ERP component indicating motor planning. In other words, it is present once the participant has made a decision and is getting ready to execute its related motor action (e.g., keypress). According to the LBA model, the nond parameter represents the sum of all non-decision processes (e.g. early perceptual processes, motor planning). Thus, it is logical to predict that (a) the LRP and nond will be positively correlated and that (b) the duration of motor programming, as assessed using the response-locked LRP will be shorter than nond. All analysis will be performed on both the emotional task, and the faces (cognitive) task. Hypothesis We hypothesize that the duration of the response-locked LRP-onset (i.e. the time window between the onset of the LRP and the response itself) will be shorter than the estimated nond, with the difference representing the duration of early perceptual processes. Moreover, we hypothesize that there will be a negative correlation between the response-locked LRP duration (as estimated using the LOTO methodology; Gluth & Meiran, 2019) and the nond. LOTO estimates are reverse, such the longer LRP duration obtained by the LOTO, represent a participant with faster LRP duration than the group. Practically, we hypothesize that longer LRP durations will be associated with smaller nond estimates. Data cleaning and analysis We will exclude from all analysis (both modeling and EEG) trials with response time (RT) shorter than 200 ms. There are no deviant participants (participants with low percent of normative responses in the emotional task or low accuracy rate in the faces task). We will exclude deviant stimuli from the emotional task. Stimuli will be excluded if the proportion of normative response is below .55. This proportion will be calculated using the data from the current as well as from previous experiment conducted on different participants (with the same methodology, but with no EEG data recorded). Stimuli excluded will be also excluded from the LRP analysis. Nond Per-subject nond will be estimated using hierarchical modeling, specifically by using the 'ggdmc' package in r. Priors will be the same priors as those used successfully in modeling this task in other experiments in the lab. Specifically: pop.mean<-c(2,2,.3,2,.5) names(pop.mean)<-GetPNames(model) pop.scale<-c(.6,.6,.1,.8,.8) names(pop.scale)<-GetPNames(model) prior.beta <- c(rep(1,npar)) names(prior.beta)<-GetPNames(model) #prior p.prior<-BuildPrior( dists = rep("tnorm", npar), p1 = pop.mean, p2 = pop.scale, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = pop.mean+pop.scale*8) mu.prior <- BuildPrior( dists = rep("tnorm", npar), p1 = pop.mean, p2 = pop.scale, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = pop.mean+pop.scale*8) sig<-c(rep(1,npar)) names(sig)<-GetPNames(model) sigma.prior<- BuildPrior( dists = rep("beta", npar), p1 = sig, p2 = sig, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = c(rep(3,npar))) LRP Data will be analyzed using a combination of routines from the EEGLAB MATLAB© toolbox (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) and custom code. Data will first be down-sampled to 250 Hz and high-pass filtered (cut-off 1Hz). Subsequently, a customized adaptive filter will be applied to suppress line-noise. This will be followed by Artifact Subspace Reconstruction (Mullen et al., 2015), re-referencing to the mean and low-pass filtering (cutoff 40Hz). Next, Infomax ICA was applied(Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). The resulting independent components (ICs) will be evaluated automatically for artifacts, by combining spatial, spectral, and temporal analysis of ICs. ICs identified as containing ocular, muscular, or cardiac artifacts will be removed from data. Based on "Detecting the onset of the lateralized readiness potential: A comparison of available methods and procedures" (Mordkoff & Gianaros, 2000), we will asses response locked LRP onset using a regression based method (their 1DF model), were we will fit 2 separate regression lines to each participant's LRP wave-form. One for the pre-onset period (constant at zero) and another for the post-onset period (a straight line connecting zero at the LRP-onset time point and peak LRP amplitude) the (single) parameter of this model is LRP-onset. As recommended by Mordkoff and Gianaros, we will use the Jackknife method to assess the SD across participants. We will use LOTO (Gluth & Meiran, 2019) to assess the rank-ordering of individuals in terms of their LRP-onset. We will then estimate the positive Pearson correlation between the LOTO estimates of LRP-onset and the ‘ggdmc’ estimates of individual nond. We will use a single t-test (Bayesian) to assess the difference between the mean ggdmc estimated nond and the average LRP-onset Bell, A. J., & Sejnowski, T. J. (1995). oer_title: Qualitative analysis of measurement reactivity in an experience sampling study
oer_summary: Content: Hypotheses Design Plan Sampling Plan Variables Prior Knowledge of Data Analysis Plan Other Hypotheses This research is exploratory, we have no hypotheses for this analysis. Design Plan Study type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials. Blinding No blinding is involved in this study. Is there any additional blinding in this study? Participants did not know the intervention group to which they had been assigned. At the beginning of the study, participants did know that there were groups that differ in the amount of time they need to invest and in the incentive they receive (this was stated on the informed consent), but they were not informed about the nature of the other groups. Control questions were included at the end of the study to be able to see to what extent participants were aware of the study hypotheses (see supplementary materials for questions in Dutch). Study design All study procedures have been approved by the Social and Societal Ethics Committee at KU Leuven. A baseline session was followed by a 14 day ESM period. After the ESM period participants returned to the lab for a follow-up session. The individual parts of the study are described in the following paragraphs in more detail. Baseline session After providing informed consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of the six experimental conditions and asked to fill out the baseline questionnaires (previous or current psychopathology, alcohol use, smoking, drug use, demographics & contact information, smartphone use, personality, depression, anxiety, self-esteem, emotion regulation, perceived stress, & momentary and trait affect; all questionnaires that were developed or adapted for this study are provided in the supplementary materials). The six conditions were: a short ESM questionnaire 3 times per day, a short ESM questionnaire 6 times per day, a short ESM questionnaire 9 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 3 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 6 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 9 times per day. The short questionnaire consisted of ± 30 items (depending on branching logic) and the long questionnaire consisted of ± 60 items (depending on branching logic; both questionnaires can be found in the supplementary materials in the original Dutch form and translated to English). Participants were briefed individually about the ESM testing period (the briefing script can be found in the supplementary materials) and practiced filling in the ESM questionnaire to assure that all items were understood by the participants. The briefing lasted approximately 20 minutes. As determined by the randomization procedure, participants were also told how many times per day they would be signaled to complete the questionnaire and how much money they would receive for their participation (the incentive was dependent on the condition; participants in the conditions with 3 beeps per day received 40 euro, while those in the 6 and 9 beep conditions received 60 and 80 euro, respectively). The briefing was conducted in Dutch or English, depending on the researcher conducting the session. 14 Days of ESM The lab visit was followed by the ESM testing period of 14 days. During this time, participants, depending on the experimental condition, received 3, 6, or 9 prompts per day to fill in a short or long questionnaire. Participants had the option to contact the researchers in case of problems. Posttest session After the two weeks of ESM, a second session was conducted during which participants were asked to fill out the posttest questionnaires (burden, social norm & ideal affect, depression, anxiety, self-esteem, emotion regulation, momentary and retrospective affect; all questionnaires that were created or adapted for this study are provided in the supplementary materials). A (randomly chosen) subsample of approximately 10 participants per experimental condition was invited to a qualitative interview lasting approximately 10 minutes, at the end of the posttest session. The qualitative interview was semi-structured, in the sense that participants were asked a series of predetermined questions and follow-up questions were asked depending on the answers (a list of the questions can be found in the supplementary materials). All participants received their compensation and were debriefed about the study after the posttest session. During the debriefing, it was explained that the study consisted of different groups that received different numbers of beeps per day and different questionnaires (see supplementary materials). Participants received 40, 60, or 80 euro in form of gift vouchers depending on the number of beeps per day. The amounts of the incentives were decided during focus groups and based on experiences of researchers with student recruitment at KU Leuven in the past, as well as the available budget. We reduced the incentive to 25, 30, and 40 euro if a participant responded to less than a third of the scheduled beeps during the study (i.e., to less than 14, 28, and 42 beeps in the 3, 6, and 9 beep conditions, respectively). The reduced amount corresponds to the full payment for both lab sessions (20 euro) plus roughly a third of the payment for the ESM period (no exact payments were possible because the payments needed to be made in vouchers of 5 euro). Participants were informed about the existence of a minimum compliance requirement during the briefing, but not about the exact requirement (this sentence was used in the briefing: “If we find that you didn’t fill in enough beeps, you will not get the full payment at the end.”; for the full instructions please see the supplementary materials). Randomization A total of 163 participant were randomly assigned to an experimental condition (see Section sample size for details). Randomization into the different conditions was based on a scheme that ensured that an equal number of participants in each condition started on every day of the week (participants could start on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday). This measure was taken to prevent that time effects would be driven by weekday (e.g., if all participants in one group would start on a Tuesday, a drop of compliance on the 5th ESM day could be purely driven by the fact that the 5th ESM day was always a Saturday; starting a roughly equal number of participants from every condition on every weekday was supposed to assure that these effects cancel out). Ten participants per experimental condition were randomly selected to take part in the qualitative interview. Sampling Plan Existing data Registration following analysis of the data: Part of the data collected during this study have been accessed and analyzed for research questions unrelated to the current investigation, as described under prior knowledge of the data. Specify whether this data is open or publicly available: Data are not publicly available. ESM data collection procedure The ESM period lasted 14 days and was signal contingent. Participants received 3, 6, or 9 beeps, depending on the condition they have been assigned to during the baseline session. Beeps were semi-randomly spread between 9 am and 10:30 pm. In the 3-beep condition, beeps were scheduled randomly in each of three 4 h 30 min windows. In the 6-beep condition, the day was split into six 2 h 15 min windows and a beep was scheduled randomly in each of the windows. In the 9-beep condition, the day was split into 9 1h 30 min windows and one beep scheduled in each of them. There was a no beep window of 20 minutes between consecutive beeps. On day 3, 6, 9, and 12, an instructed response item (i.e., a trick item that was supposed to function as a test if participants were paying attention to the questionnaire) was added to one of the questionnaires. It was always presented at the middle beep in the 3 beep condition and switched between the third and fourth beep in the 6 beep condition. In the 9 beep condition, it was shown once at the fourth beep, once at the sixth beep, and twice at the fifth beep. Due to constraints by the program used, no no-beep window of 20 minutes could be guaranteed between the last beep before the questionnaire with the instructed response item and the questionnaire with instructed response item (i.e., the last beep before the beep with the instructed response item could be less than 20 minutes before the beep with the instructed response item). The same applies to the first questionnaire after the questionnaire with the instructed response item. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a short (~30 items) or long questionnaire (~60 items) during the study. The ESM questionnaires can be found in the supplementary materials. Following a pilot test, we estimated the completion time for the short questionnaire to be around 1,5 min and 2,5 min for the long questionnaire. The phone beeped or vibrated for 90 seconds or until the participant started filling in the questionnaire. After 90 seconds, the questionnaire became unavailable. Once participants started filling in the questionnaire, they had 90 seconds until time out per question (in case of time out, the questionnaire stopped and no subsequent questions were shown). Participants received a phone (motorola DEFY+) with the app mobileQ (Meers et al., 2019) installed on it. Other functions of the phone were fully disabled. At every beep, a start screen of the questionnaire was displayed automatically (see Figure 2). Participants had to press “start survey” on this start screen to proceed to the first question. Sound and vibration could be turned on and off separately by the participants, but they couldn’t be disabled at the same time (if sound was switched off, the vibration was turned on automatically). Notifications did not require an internet connection to be delivered. Sample size (number of participants) Overall study: We aimed to recruit 150 students for the study. Participants were eligible for inclusion if they were Dutch speaking, between 18-30 years old, currently enrolled as a student at a university or hogeschool, and had never taken part in a study that used a phone app before. Participants were recruited via advertisements on Facebook groups for research participants and flyers that were placed on different campuses of KU Leuven and in local bars. Recruitment started on 17.12.18 and testing was conducted between 11.02.19 and 18.07.19. Of the 164 participants that took part in the baseline session, 3 participants had to be excluded because they were not currently enrolled as a student, 2 dropped out during the ESM period, 4 missed more than 1 full day of data because of technical problems (for one participant the battery of the phone broke, for 3 people the time of the phone was reset for unknown reasons which led to beeps not being delivered), for 2 participants the time on the phone was off by more than 1 hour (which lead to the beeps being delivered at wrong times), and 1 participant failed to meet the minimum compliance requirement of one third of the ESM questionnaires started). For all these participants new participants were recruited. The reasoning for this decision was to assure that we would have at least 25 participants per condition in all analyses. Since it was uncertain whether technical problems would appear or participants would complete the study, more participants were included than our original inclusion goal. As soon as it was clear that every group had 25 ‘valid’ cases, no further participants were recruited. Sample used for current analysis: Originally, a subsample of 60 participants (10 per experimental condition) were randomly chosen to take part in a qualitative interview after the end of the ESM period. Some interviews were not conducted due to scheduling problems (e.g., several participants were at the lab at the same time, which made it impossible to conduct a particular interview) or due to exclusion or drop out of participants after randomization. 52 of the planned interviews were conducted. Due to a technical problem during one of the interviews, no recording of this interview is available. Therefore, 51 transcribed interviews are available for analysis. Sample size rationale The overall sample for this study was based on power calculations for a previous analysis of the dataset. Based on practical considerations (i.e. the time needed to conduct and analyze interviews), we chose to interview a subset of 60 participants. This sample was expected to be large enough to obtain a thorough understanding of different experiences of participants during this ESM study. Variables Notes: Only the data used in the current preregistration are described. More information on other data that were collected during this study can be found in the supplementary material and other registrations of the project "The effects of sampling frequency and questionnaire length on perceived burden, compliance, and careless responding in ESM data in a student population". Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a randomly chosen subsample of 52 participants (see sample size for further details). The interviews were conducted in English by Mariam Chichua (master student working on the project), and in Dutch by Tessa Biesemans (research assistant) and G.E.. They were recorded and transcribed (verbatim) by several interns and G.E.. All transcriptions were checked for accuracy by G.E.. At the beginning of the interviews, participants were instructed to talk about their experiences during the ESM study. It was stated that the interview would be based on prepared questions, but participants were encouraged to also report other experiences that were not included in the questions. In an effort to reduce social desirability, it was stressed that there were no right or wrong answers. The semi-structured interviews included the following questions, which were based on the broader literature on ESM: What was it like to fill in the questionnaires in the beginning? What was it like in the end? Do you think you filled the questionnaires in differently depending on whether someone else was around or depending on your location? How? Do you think that filling in the questionnaires had an influence on you? If yes, in what way? Did you learn something about yourself during the study? What do you think about the study? How easy was it to remember how you felt before the beep? Did you ever answer that the beep disturbed you? [If yes] Can you describe in what way you were disturbed? You know that our goal is to better understand people’s daily lives. If you were to set up a smartphone study, what would you do differently? Did you find it difficult at some moments to fill in the questionnaires? Why? Were there moments when you were not able to respond? Can you describe why? Can you explain how you used the following questions during the last week? - It cost effort to answer to the questions - I filled in the questions attentively - Since the last time you filled in a questionnaire were you aware that you missed a beep? (missing data) Why did you not respond? Please select all that applies o I could not respond (on time); o I did not want to respond; o I was too stressed to respond; o I felt burdened by the beep; o Other reason Prior knowledge of data The following analyses of data from this study have been conducted: a. The effects of sampling frequency and questionnaire length on burden, compliance, and careless responding in a student population. https://osf.io/pzx8r/. Compliance and careless responding is known across the different experimental groups. Additionally, information on patterns of missed beeps, temporal increases or decreases in burden over the time of the study, and the use of the objective careless responding item was extracted from the interviews and included in this publication. b. oer_title: Relations between self-regulation, delinquency and psychopathology from adolescence to adulthood
oer_summary: Data have been made available to the researchers, the following things have been done since: - Files have been compiled - Scores have been calculated for each measure Self-regulation: cognitive, emotional and behavioral Deviance: parent, teacher, self Psychopathology: mood, anxiety and eating disorder symptom count - Missing data were inspected, as a reasonably large amount of participants had missing data at one or more time points it was necessary to look at this more closely. - Data was inspected visually using the ExPanD function from R’s ExPanDaR package for exploring panel data - ICC’s were calculated for the different scales over time - Correlations were inspected for the deviance measures with overlapping timepoints - As the ICC for the teacher measures was low (ICC2 = .27) and correlations with parents at time 2 (r = .34) and with youth at time 3 (r = .19) were lower than for example correlations between parent at time 2 and youth at time 3 (r = .42), the decision was made to not use the teacher reports and only use parent and youth self-report for the deviance measure. Teachers’ scores may have been less reliable due to the limited possibility for students to exhibit these types of antisocial behaviors during class, as well as the limited time teachers spend with students in class (at time 3 students were in secondary school and might have had little time with a single teacher). - For further updates, see sections marked UPDATE below. 1. Research questions 1) Does self-regulation remain stable from early adolescence to adulthood? 2) To what extent can self-regulation causally predict deviance throughout adolescence and adulthood? 3) To what extent can self-regulation longitudinally predict psychopathology? 4) To what extent are there reciprocal relations between self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time? 2. Hypotheses 1) There is medium to high stability of self-regulation over time. There is less stability of self-regulation in vulnerable groups. 2) Low self-regulation predicts deviance over adolescence and adulthood. 3) Low self-regulation predicts psychopathology over adolescence and adulthood. 4) There are reciprocal relations between low self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time (i.e., low self-regulation predicts deviance/psychopathology which in turn predicts low self-regulation at the next time point). 3. Data The current study will make use of existing data from a large longitudinal study conducted by CEDAR. The data was not accessible by the researchers at time of registration, coding books were available and one researcher had previously used other parts of this dataset. Researchers looked into the official criminal records in order to assess if these were useful as a measure, but did not conduct any analyses on this data. The sample consists of a group of over 900 participants that were followed from age 10-12 to age 30, during eight measurements. The precise number of participants in the group, and the amount of dropout is presently unknown, making it difficult to specify exact models for analysis. UPDATE: Data for one or more of the measures at one or more time points is available for 772 individuals. Variables of interest 1) Self-regulation A 92-item dysregulation inventory Mezzich, Tarter, Giancola, & Kirisci (2001) will be used to measure cognitive, emotional and behavioral self-regulation. This data was present at all 8 measurement points. 2) Deviance Deviance will be measured using overlapping items from the CBCL parent/teacher reports (before age 16) and the Youth/Adult self-report (after age 16). Items differ slightly across different measures, but concern the same content. Items seem to reflect major and minor deviance at face value. As double measure (i.e., parent/teacher, teacher/youth) were taken at certain time points, it will be checked if both tap in to the same underlying construct. A confirmatory factor analysis will be done to ensure all items load on a single deviance factor. The items and alternative wordings can be found below. Major deviance items | alternative wordings Destroys property belonging to (his/her family or) others | I (damage or) destroy things belonging to others Gets in many fights | I get in many fights Physically attacks people | I physically attack people Steals | I steal Threatens people | I threaten to hurt people Minor deviance items | alternative wordings Cruelty, bullying or meanness to others | I am mean to others Destroys his/her owns things | I (damage or) destroy my (own) things Doesn’t seem to feel guilty after misbehaving | I don't feel guilty after doing something I shouldn’t Hangs around with other who get in trouble | I hang around with kids/others/people who get in trouble Lying or cheating | I lie or cheat Temper tantrums or hot temper | I have a hot temper Used alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes | I use alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes; I use drugs (other than alcohol (and nicotine)) for non-medical purposes Criminal records Criminal records were consulted around 19 years of age, and will be taken in as part of the deviance measure, or as a separate construct, depending on how well these items converge. UPDATE: criminal records where not obtained and will not be used in the model. 3) Psychopathology Psychopathology was measured in a variety of ways at different time points within the data collected by CEDAR. For the current study the aim was to find a general measure of mental health functioning, rather than looking at specific mental disorder diagnoses. There are two measures in the data which might make this possible. First is the Global Assessment of Functioning scores, given by clinicians during diagnostic interviews using the Psychiatric History Marker. Second is the use of symptom counts of the SCID. Both methods have limits, the first due to the possibility of unreliable GAF scores due to the interviews being done by different clinicians. SCID symptom counts on the other hand might show large variation in severity, and when looking at individuals with similar scores, one might have a clinical disorder, where the other might have a collective of minor symptoms scattered over different disorders. UPDATE: Based on a general glance of the data, the GAF scores did not seem like a good option, as they were given infrequently and with little variation. Therefore it was decided to use the SCID items as an indicator of psychopathology. Items representing symptoms that were scored in a yes/no format were taken as indicators of psychopathology (e.g., “Have you ever been particularly nervous or anxious for an extended period of time?”). Furthermore, items that could indicate the gravity of the disorder were counted if they were in a yes/no format (i.e., for social phobia, several situations were listed in which someone could experience fear, e.g., speaking in public, the presence of fear in each of these situations was counted separately, as fear in many situations would indicate more severe psychopathology). UPDATE: The SCID is a diagnostic interview, regarding symptoms of many known mental health conditions. Data was available on Major Depression, Dysthymic Disorder, Manic Syndrome, Psychotic and Associated Symptoms, Anxiety disorders (Panic Disorder, Agoraphobia, Social Phobia, Simple Phobia, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder), Somatoform Disorders, Eating Disorders (Anorexia and Boulimia Nervosa), Adjustment Disorder, Antisocial Personality Questionnaire Supplement, Conduct Disorder Supplement. For the purpose of the current study, mood, anxiety and eating disorder items will be used, as these are sufficiently distinct from both deviance and self-regulation, but may still influence them. Based on the items present in the questionnaire, it did not seem logical to use somatoform items, as the presence of a potential medical cause is not known. With regard to Antisocial and Conduct items, there seems to be too large of an overlap with the items present in both the deviance and the self-regulation items (i.e., items concerning impulsive and criminal acts) to the point where the items would no longer be informative. With regard to psychotic symptoms, although these symptoms might lead to deviant behavior, or be caused by deviant behavior (i.e., drug use), it is not deemed sufficiently informative to aid the question asked in the current study, also a link with self-regulation is not expected. Adjustment disorder was not taken along as the items are not symptoms on their own, but refer to how well a person deals with his/her symptoms. Furthermore, combining symptoms of these different disorders is unlikely to provide us with a unidimensional, interpretable scale for psychopathology. What remains are three classes of internalizing disorders, mood, anxiety and eating disorders, that are separate from, but may be related to self-regulation (e.g., a lack of emotion regulation for mood and anxiety disorders, a lack of cognitive or behavioral regulation for eating disorders) and/or deviance (e.g., mood disorders may limit the possibilities for committing deviant acts, anxiety disorders may develop because of deviant behavior). UPDATE: The selected items of the mood, anxiety and eating disorders will be scored as 1 (present) or 0 (not present/not scored). The “not scored” part applies to items that were not scored due to the way the SCID is taken, that is, when a person answers negatively on a specific item they would not be asked questions that would specify the symptoms further (e.g., if someone has never experienced a panic attack, no further questions about panic attacks were asked). As clinicians decided it was not needed to score these items, for the purpose of the current study, they were scored as absent. The symptom count will be averaged for mood, anxiety and eating disorders separately, and then averaged on total. Averaging on disorder level was done to avoid the number of items for a single disorder to affect the total score for a participant, as some disorders had more items assessing smaller aspects of the disorder. 4. Analyses (preliminary) In order to inspect basic stability of self-regulation over time, Spearman’s rank order correlations will be used. Correlation coefficients of the vulnerable and general group will be transformed and compared to each other. A cross-lagged panel design using structural equation modeling will be used to inspect the relations between the different variables over time for the whole group (as the underlying mechanisms should be the same). Two theoretical models will be compared for model fit, one with only effects of self-regulation on crime/psychopathology and one with reciprocal relationships. Changes may be made in an exploratory way in order to improve model fit. UPDATE: The cross-lagged panel design will be tested using a Random Intercept Cross Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) using structural equation modeling. This will be done in R, using the Lavaan package. In the RI-CLPM latent factors are calculated for each construct over measurement points, with the weight of each regression set to 1. This is done to remove between-person effects from the model, so that within-person changes can be observed. Missing data will be estimated using the full information maximum likelihood (FIML) method, which is present in the Lavaan package, when running the SEM model (most likely using a robust version for non-normal data, i.e., MLR). UPDATE: As on first inspection of the variables there was little variance in the psychopathology measure (i.e., most people did not show any signs of psychopathology), it was decided to run and compare a model with only self-regulation and deviance, and a full model including psychopathology. As one model is nested in the other, it will be possible to compare both models statistically. After the best of both models is selected, adjustments might be made in an exploratory way, to improve model fit.

oer_title: The Pervasive Impact of Ignorance
oer_summary: 1) Have any data been collected for this study already? No, no data have been collected for the study yet. 2) What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested in this study? Previous research has shown that a host of different judgments are influenced by norm violations (e.g., acting immorally). We plan to ask whether these effects are moderated by whether or not the agent was ignorant of the relevant norm that was being violated. Below, we quickly describe each previous study, or manipulation and the relevant predictions. Phillips & Knobe, 2009: Previously, this research found that participants rated a ship captain as less forced to throw something overboard if throwing that thing overboard was immoral (e.g., passengers) vs. not immoral (e.g., cargo). Here, we manipulate whether the ship captain is reasonably ignorant of what he is throwing overboard, and thus whether or not the action is immoral. We predict that the difference in force judgments between the ignorant immoral (unaware of passengers) and neutral (cargo) conditions will be smaller than the difference between the informed immoral and neutral conditions, or that there will be no difference. Fraser & Knobe, 2008 Previously, this research found that when administrative assistants are allowed to take pens and professors are not, if both an administrative assistant and a professor take the last two pens, participants agreed that the professor was more of a cause of the problem than the administrative assistant. We manipulate whether the professor is ignorant that she is doing something wrong. We predict that the difference in causal judgements between the ignorant immoral (not knowing they’re not allowed to take pen) and neutral (allowed to take pen) conditions will be smaller than the difference between informed immoral and neutral causal judgements. Cushman, Knobe, & Sinnott Armstrong, 2008 Previously, this research found that participants are more likely to say that a doctor who has stated his dislike of homeless people, ended a homeless man's life (vs. allowed it to end) when the doctor acted immorally (disconnecting the homeless man from a ventilator to avoid wasting time and resources) compared to when the doctor acted neutrally (disconnecting the man from the ventilator to preserve his dignity). In both cases, the man will die in a week or two no matter what the doctor does. We manipulate whether the doctor is ignorant of whether or not the man is homeless. We predict that the difference in the extent to which participants judge the doctor to have ended (vs. allowed to end) the homeless man’s life will be smaller between the ignorant immoral (unaware the man is homeless) and neutral condition than in the informed immoral and neutral conditions. Knobe, 2003: Previously, this research found that participants were much more likely to judge a chairman as bringing about a side-effect of a new program intentionally if that side effect is morally bad (e.g., harming the environment) than when it is morally good (e.g., helping the environment), though the chairman expressed that he only cares about the program’s profits in both conditions. We additionally manipulate whether the chairman and everyone in the company are ignorant to the true environmental impact of the new program. We predict that the difference in judgements of the chairman’s intentionality in bringing about the side effects between the immoral (harming the environment) and neutral (helping the environment) conditions will be weaker when the vice president is ignorant of the harmful environmental impact. Phillips et al., 2015: Previously, this research found that when agents are living a morally bad life (e.g., a nurse poisoning sick children), participants rated those agents as less happy than those acting morally (e.g., a nurse helping sick children) even though the agents mental states were uniformly described as satisfying the criteria for happiness. We manipulate whether the nurse is ignorant that she is doing something wrong. We predict that the difference in judgements of the nurse’s happiness between the immoral (harming children) and neutral (helping children) conditions will be lesser when the nurse is ignorant of the fact that what she is doing is wrong. Young and Phillips, 2011 Previously, this research found that participants more agreed with the active form of the sentence “The captain forced the sailor…” than the passive form of the sentence “The sailor was forced by the captain…” but only when the action the captain pressured the sailor to do was immoral. We manipulate whether the captain and sailor are ignorant of the immorality of the action and we predict that when the captain and sailor are both ignorant, this effect is weaker: that participants will more equally judge that the captain forced the sailor to the action and that the sailor was forced by the captain to do the action (i.e., smaller or no difference in the force judgments). Young and Phillips, 2011 Previously, this research found that participants agree more with the active form of the sentence “The chief forced the doctor...” than the passive form of the sentence “The doctor was forced by the chief...” when the action the chief pressured the doctor to do was immoral (e.g., kill the patient). We manipulate whether the chief and doctor are ignorant of the immorality of the action and predict that the effect of active v. passive forms of sentences on perceived fault is weaker when the chief and doctor are ignorant. Kominsky & Phillips, 2019; Icard, et al., 2017 Previously this research has found (across four different scenarios) that when an agent acts immorally and contributes to an outcome, people judge that agent to be more of a cause of the outcome (and find changes to that agent’s actions to be more counterfactually relevant) than another agent who acted morally but whose action was also necessary for the outcome to occur (e.g., in a conjunctive causal structure). In contrast to this condition in which both actions were necessary, the agent who acted immorally is judged to be less of a cause of the outcome if both agents’ actions are independently sufficient to bring about the outcome (i.e., a disjunctive causal structure). We created new conditions in which the agents are not aware that they are acting immorally, and predict that in these conditions, both effects will weaken: In both the conjunctive and disjunctive causal structures, participants causal judgments will show less of a difference between the two agents. Petitt & Knobe, 2009 Previously, this research found that the impact of moral judgement plays a role in the application of many concepts that involves holding or displaying a positive attitude toward an outcome, specifically intentional action, desire, ‘decided’, and arbitrary expressions of positive attitude (‘advocated’ and ‘in favor of’). Likewise, they find attributions of negative attitudes like opposition are weaker when an outcome is morally bad vs good. We manipulate whether the agent in a vignette is ignorant that they are acting immorally, and predict that when the agent is ignorant, the pervasive effect of moral judgement is weaker: participants will disagree more that the agent was holding or displaying a positive attitude to the negative side effect (and disagree less to the agent holding a negative attitude) when the agent is ignorant of that side-effect than when the agent knows that the chosen action will have that side-effect. Szabo & Knobe, 2003 Previously, this research demonstrated that the effect of norm violations found in previous research on force, intention, causation extended to ‘modal proxies’ of these judgments. For example, just as people would say an agent was more forced to do a morally neutral action than an immoral action, they more agreed with the sentence ‘Given the circumstances, the agent had to do that action’ when the action was morally neutral than when the action was immoral. We ask whether both these effects on the relevant modal proxies are affected by the agent’s knowledge of the norm. Specifically, we predict that when the agent is ignorant that their action will have a negative consequence, agreement with the modal proxies will differ from the case in which the agent knew that the action would have a negative consequence (and be more similar to the cases in which the agents’ actions did not have a negative consequence). Uttich and Lombrozo, 2010 Previously, this research found that participants agreed it was more appropriate to say an agent brought about a side effect intentionally in norm-violating cases than in norm-conforming cases for both moral and conventional norm violations. We manipulate whether the agent is ignorant that they are violating a conventional norm. We predict that the difference in judgement of intentionality between the ignorant norm violating and the neutral condition will be smaller than in the intentional norm violating and neutral conditions. 3) Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured. We outline each dependent variable for each relevant study below: Phillips & Knobe 2009 Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “The ship captain was forced to cut the cargo loose and let it fall into the sea.” On a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). In all conditions, participants will be also asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “The captain knew that a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.” and “The captain should have known whether or not a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Fraser & Knobe, 2008 Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “Prof. Smith caused the problem.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “Prof. Smith knew that only administrative assistants are allowed to take pens.” and “Prof. Smith should have known whether or not only administrative assistants are allowed to take pens.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Cushman, Knobe, & Sinnott Armstrong, 2008 Participants will indicate their tendency concerning the following sentence: “Is it more appropriate to say that Dr. Bennett ended the homeless man’s life, or that he allowed it to end?” On a scale from 1 (Allowed to end) to 7 (Ended). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “Dr. Bennett knew that the man in front of him was a homeless person.” and “Dr. Bennett should have known whether or not the man in front of him was a homeless person.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Knobe, 2003: Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “The chairman of the board intentionally helped [harmed] the environment.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “The chairman knew that the program harms the environment.” and “The chairman should have known whether or not the program harms the environment” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Phillips et al., 2015 Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “Sarah is happy.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “Sarah knew that the gummy vitamins contain pesticides.” and “Sarah should have known whether or not the gummy vitamins contain pesticides.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In the passive conditions, participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “The sailor was forced by the captain to cut the cargo loose and let it fall into the sea.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Participants will be randomly assigned to see three conditions in random order (one non-norm violation condition, one knowledgeable norm violation condition, and one ignorant norm violation condition). We will aim to collect >30 responses for each dependent variable in each study being replicated and extended. In the original studies, there are 27 key comparisons that we will aim to replicate and extend. Thus, we plan to collect 1500 participants, which should give us an average of ~55 responses per dependent variable. 5) Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct to examine the main question/hypothesis. Primary Analysis: First, we will ask, in each individual study, whether we replicated the originally observed effect. In all cases where we are able to replicate the original effect, we will then do the same statistical test, but replace the original knowledgeable norm-violation condition with the new ignorant norm-violation condition. Our hypothesis is that the effect sizes (all converted to r) for the second analysis will be smaller than the for the first analysis. Given this, our statistical approach will be meta-analytic: to statistically investigate whether our hypothesis is correct, we will collect the effect sizes from both our replications of the original statistical tests and the new statistical tests involving the ignorance conditions and analyze them by comparing a series of linear mixed-effects models (implemented in the lme4 package in R). More specifically, we will build a model that predicts effects sizes with a fixed effect for whether the non-norm violation condition was compared to a knowledge norm-violation or an ignorant norm violation (call this fixed effect “epistemicState”). This model will also include random intercepts and slopes for the paradigm that was being replicated and extended (epistemicState | paradigm) and perhaps (epistemicState | participant) -- and then simplify down to just a random intercept for paradigm or participant in case of convergence problems. We will then compare this model to one that does not include the fixed effect “epistemicState” but is otherwise identical (including the random effects structure) using the anova function in R. Secondary analyses: In addition, we will also analyze both knowledge questions that were included as dependent variables. Our key question with these additional dependent variables is whether either or both of them mediate the effect of “epistemicState” hypothesized above. Accordingly, we will calculate the effect size for the difference for both the “knows” and “should know” questions in a manner similar to the primary analysis. We will first conduct the statistical tests from the original paper but now on responses to the “knows” questions, comparing the non-norm violation conditions to the knowledgeable norm violation conditions. Secondly, we will then conduct an identical set of statistical tests but compare the non-norm violation conditions to the ignorant norm violation conditions.
