oer_title: Behavioural Consistency in Smartphone Use
oer_summary: Behavioural Consistency in Application Use Background: The proposed research aims to assess whether digital traces of behaviour, specifically smartphone use, show within-person consistency across time and context. Time in this project is defined as different days of the week, and context is defined as the specific application a person is using. Using pre-existing data sets, which collected smartphone use from the same person over several days, it is possible to assess if application usage time, and application number of pickups is consistent across apps (context) and across days (time). We will mirror work conducted by Shoda, Mischel, & Wright, (1994) which outlines how to create intraindividual situation-behaviour profiles and further assess the similarity in the ‘shapes’ of these profiles across days of data from each person. Data: We have obtained app usage data from several datasets. This included the LiveLab dataset, (Shepard, Rahmati, Tossell, Zhong, & Kortum, 2011), the Consumer Mobile Experience dataset (OFCOM, 2019), the Securacy dataset (Jones, Ferreira, Hosio, Goncalves, & Kostakos, 2015), the Mobile Phone Usage (MPU) dataset (Pielot et al., 2017), Health and Smartphone Use dataset (Shaw, Ellis, Geyer, Ziegler, & Davidson, 2018), the Tsinghu App datset (Yu, Li, Xu, Zhang, & Kostakos, 2018), the CARAT dataset (Oliner, Iyer, Stoica, Lagerspetz, & Tarkoma, 2013), the Student Life dataset (Wang et al., 2014) and the Mobile Data Challenge (MDC) dataset (Kiukkonen, Blom, Dousse, Gatica-perez, & Laurila, 2010). We established some inclusion criteria to assess suitability of these datasets. Specifically, datasets had to contain time stamps of foreground application use so we could examine what application was on screen (a person’s context) at each time, and for how long. Consequently, four of these datasets were unsuitable for our analysis. The Tsinghu App dataset only included app categories and not the specific applications used. The CARAT dataset had data whereby lots of applications were documented as being used at the same time, including multiple simultaneous foreground applications. Therefore, it was difficult to establish which application was on the screen and being used at each time stamp. The Student Life dataset only recorded running applications and not foreground application use. Finally, it was only possible in the Mobile Data Challenge (MDC) dataset to determine when a new app appeared in the foreground, but not when the use of that particular app ended due to a lack of screen state data. The remaining datasets required standardisation so they could be combined and analysed as a single dataset. All datasets were converted to this format, with these column headers: PersonID, DataSet, Application, Start_Time_Stamp, End_Time_Stamp, Duration_Sec, Age, Gender. Each row represented a single app use event. The steps to do this standardisation included: Stage 1: 1. Unix timestamps were converted to ‘human readable’ timestamps which represented the local time (rather than universal time) for each participant. 2. Within the datasets which had Age data; Age was converted from an interval variable to a categorical variable with these categories: 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55+. This was to match data from the Consumer Mobile Experience dataset which contained age data to this categorical resolution. 3. Character data specifying gender was converted to either “MALE” or “FEMALE’. 4. Durations of each app event were calculated if this was not already a variable in the dataset. 5. Duration data was converted to seconds and rounded to two decimal places. 6. If not present in the original dataset, End_Time_Stamp was calculated as follow: Start_Time_Stamp + Duration_Sec. 7. Data was ordered by Person ID and Start_Time_Stamp. Stage 2 – For the 100 most used applications: 1. Chrome and Browser were re-categorised as ‘Internet’ to establish uniformity no matter what browser application was native to each type of smartphone. 2. Package names e.g. “com.facebook.katana’ were converted to human readable names e.g. “Facebook”. 3. Different brands had different package names for their native clock app. All were converted to “Clock”. 4. Removed data from people who had less than 9 days of data and less than 9 app events. This left 824 people in the sample. 5. For each person, removed data from the first and last day of their data. This insured only full days were measured. 6. Removed any events that had a duration that was a negative number. 7. For the final combined dataset, only included applications that were used by over 25% of the same (>206 people) and applications which were not system apps. Analysis to pre-register: Following processing, we have a final dataset of 820 people with longitudinal (>7 days) application data. Following the procedure of Shoda, Mischel, & Wright, (1994), it is possible to create daily behaviour profiles of application use. The consistency of these daily behaviour profiles can be assessed within the same person by comparing their behaviour profiles across the many days of data we have for that person. Daily behaviour profiles can be created for 2 types of smartphone behaviours; daily app time, and daily app number of pickups. This requires the generation of 2 new datasets for each participant: Daily App Time Dataset 1. Isolate data from X participant. 2. Remove days of data where none of the 21 apps were used. 3. Calculate for each app the daily total usage time in seconds across all days of data that we have for that person. 4. Ensure that this daily calculation accounts for switching to and from Daylight saving time. The start and ends of each day will be adjusted accordingly. Daily App Pickups Dataset 1. Isolate data from X participant. 2. Remove days of data where none of the 21 apps were used. 3. Calculate for each app the daily total number of pickups (as a count/frequency) across all days of data that we have for that person. 4. Ensure that this daily calculation accounts for switching to and from Daylight saving time. The start and ends of each day will be adjusted accordingly. Independently for each smartphone behaviour, behaviour profiles for each person will be created as follows: 1. Place everyone’s daily usage data together into one dataset column wise. This means that each row in the dataset will represent one of the 21 apps, and each column will represent a person and a day of their data (e.g. Person 1, Day 1). 2. A normative profile of daily application usage for the 21 apps will be calculated by averaging each row. 3. Standard deviations will also be calculated for each row. Then, to make a behaviour profile for a particular person and day: 1. Extract data from person X, day X. 2. Subtract the normative profile from person X, day X. 3. Then scale this by dividing these new values by the standard deviations for each app (see above) that were calculated from everyone’s data. Behaviour profiles per day can be compared within participants by conducting ipsative correlations (see Shoda et al., 1994). Scaled values from the 21 apps from person X day X can be compared to scaled values from person X day Y using correlations. However, prior to conducting the correlations, the scaled daily usage values per app will be converted to ranks (Lowest used app = 1, Highest used app = 21). Higher consistency in the ranks across days would equate to higher coefficients. Therefore, the correlation coefficient essentially reflects the stability of the rank order among the interpersonal situations (apps) within the same individual and furthermore how an individual’s usage in each situation (app) deviates from the respective normative usage of each app. It is predicted that: Hypothesis 1: Within-person smartphone use across days will be statistically and significantly higher than between-person smartphone use across days. Hypothesis 2: There will be consistency in smartphone usage across weekdays and weekends, resulting in an ipsative correlation co-efficient of .8 or higher. Confirmatory Analysis – Inferential Statistics: 1. We will test consistency using two kinds of behavioural profiles: day pairs and split halves. Day pairs will involve a selection of two random daily use profiles from the data set, on which an ipsative correlation is calculated. Split halves will involve the same comparison but calculated on an average of 50% of the individual’s daily profiles. That is, we will average the use profile over half of the individual’s data where the days averaged are selected randomly. This 50% profile will then be compared to another 50% profile (of either the same user or different user) using an ipsative correlation. We use the Split halves both because of the potential for high variation in daily usage and because some users will have more day profiles than others, and therefore have a greater influence on the day pairs analysis. 2. The ipsative correlations derived from the Day Pair and Split Halve comparisons will provide the data for permutation tests. Specifically, for the Day pairs, we will compare the distribution of correlations from between-subject pairs with the distribution of correlations from within-subject pairs (i.e., compare random pairs to pairs associated with the same user). For the Split halves, we will undertake the same comparison but use the Split half average data. We will run ~3,000,000 comparisons, which will provide approximately 10 samplings of each potential permutation (using the formula n(n-1))/2 to determine the exact amount). Exploratory analysis 1. To visualise if…then… patterns of behaviour for each person, conditional inference decision trees will be conducted with application name as the criterion variable and the daily usage statistic (either daily pickups or daily usage time) for each app as the independent variable. Data used to train the tree can either be from one person (intraindividual situation-behaviour profile), or from all people (normative profile).

oer_title: Childhood Obesity and Stigma toward Parents
oer_summary: In Study 1, we asked: (1) Do social perceivers stigmatize parents of children (here, daughters) with obesity more than parents of average/healthy-weight children? (We expect this.) (2) Does stigma transfer from obese children to average-weight parents (as a stigma-by-association account might predict)? (We did not expect this, but we found some support for it.) (3) Does parent gender moderate stigma toward parents of obese children, such that mothers are more stigmatized? (We predicted this and found some support.) (4) Might this be driven by perceptions that mothers (vs. fathers) are relatively more responsible for offspring appearance/weight? (We explored this and found instead that perceptions that parents of children with obesity [vs. average/healthy-weight] possess negative parenting qualities drove stigmatization.) In Study 2, we aim to replicate those findings and extend this to exploring sons as well as daughters.

oer_title: Childhood Obesity and Stigma toward Parents
oer_summary: In this study, we ask: (1) Do social perceivers stigmatize parents of children with obesity more than parents of average-weight children? (We expect this.) (2) Does stigma transfer from obese children to average-weight parents (as a stigma-by-association account might predict)? (We do not expect this.) (3) Does parent gender moderate stigma toward parents of obese children (such that mothers are more stigmatized), and might this be driven by perceptions that mothers (vs. fathers) are relatively more responsible for offspring appearance/weight? (We explore this.) To explore these questions, Ps are randomly assigned to view one of four stimuli of a mother or father with her/his obese or average-weight daughter. We then ask for feelings toward and inferences about the target parent. To assess stigma in general, we use liking, disliking, and a feeling thermometer. To assess stigma as a parent, we ask about the target being, e.g., a good parent, and we also assess inferences about the target as a parent (e.g., overindulgent To assess a stigma-by-association account, we ask about inferences that the target parent herself/himself, though average-weight, is deemed to have characteristics associated with obesity (e.g., lacks willpower). To assess expectations of parental responsibility for offspring weight, we use one series of items adapted from Sikorski and colleagues (2012) work that parses responsibility for weight---here using parent responsibility, child's own responsibility, societal and cultural factors, genetic factors---and a second items that asks participants to allocate a budget of 100 points to the causal thrust of these four factors for Emma's appearance/weight. We will remove participants who, e.g., fail the CAPTCHA, attention check questions from analyses. oer_title: Appreciation and Perceived Division of Labor
oer_summary: Study Rationale and Aims The aim of the current study was to assess the roles that (a) feeling appreciative for one’s partner and (b) feeling appreciated by one’s partner play in how people perceive the division of labor (DoL) in their household and associations with satisfaction with DoL and overall relationship satisfaction. More specifically, we are interested in four questions: 1. Does feeling appreciative for one’s partner predict seeing one’s partner as doing a greater share of DoL? 2. Does feeling appreciative for one’s partner moderate the association between one’s own perceptions of DoL and one’s partner’s report of DoL, such that the association between own and partner DoL is stronger (more agreement) for those who feel more (vs less) appreciative of their partner? 3. Does feeling appreciated by a partner moderate the association between perceived DoL and satisfaction with DoL? That is, perceiving that one does a greater share of the DoL could be associated with feeling less satisfied with the DoL, but is this effect attenuated if people feel more (vs less) appreciated by their partners? 4. Does feeling appreciated by one’s partner moderate the relationship between perceived DoL and relationship quality? That is, perceiving that one does a greater share of the DoL could be associated with lower relationship satisfaction, but is this effect attenuated if people feel more (vs less) appreciated by their partners? We explain these predictions and intended analyses in the planned analyses section below. This study is part of a larger study on cohabiting couples coping during the COVID-19 pandemic conducted by the Well-being, Health, and Interpersonal Relationships Lab (WHIRLab) at the University of Michigan and as such, includes many other variables of interest. Sociodemographic information was also collected at background. SEE ATTACHED ANALYSIS PLAN FOR FULL PREREGISTRATION OF ANALYSES.

oer_title: Longitudinal associations between prosocial skills and behavioral problems across childhood
oer_summary: A narrative summary of the project follows below. See the attached word-document for the full preregistration (adjusted from the Social Psychology preregistration of Van 't Veer & Giner-Sorolla, 2016). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ A broad range of studies has shown that prosocial skills and behavioral problems are related constructs. Between persons, children and adolescents higher in prosocial skills are usually lower in behavioral problems such as externalizing and internalizing problems (Flynn et al., 2015; Memmott-Elison et al., 2020). These studies indicate that prosocial skills might be a protective factor for developing behavioral problems and therefore several researchers have suggested that prosocial skills might be an interesting target in interventions for behavioral problems. However, little research has been done on within-person changes of prosocial skills and behavioral problems over time. Put otherwise, do changes within a person in one construct affect performance on the other construct? This is a crucial question with respect to intervention planning. To our knowledge, studies investigating this question so far mainly focused on within-person changes during adolescence (Padilla-Walker et al., 2015; Padilla-Walker et al., 2018). For instance, Padilla-Walker et al. (2018) showed that prosocial behavior and aggression were negatively associated bi-directionally over time. However, since prosocial behavior is a relatively stable trait once developed (Nantel-Vivier et al., 2009; Flynn et al., 2015), it might be important to investigate within-person changes in an earlier phase, during childhood. Moreover, until now it remains unclear whether there are sensitive windows for within-person changes. It is often suggested that early intervention (i.e., during early childhood) results in the largest effect. However, one might suggest that middle childhood is a more suitable period for such within-person changes, as this is a developmental phase where the first friendships emerge and prosocial skills become specifically important (Del Giudice et al., 2009; van der Meulen et al., 2018). To shed light on these important questions, the current project proposes to use random-intercept cross lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al. (2015) to investigate within person effects of prosocial skills on behavioral problems (either internalizing or externalizing) and vice versa during childhood, see Figure 1. To obtain robust results, three indicators of prosocial skills will be used: parental report of prosocial skills (SDQ); parental report of empathy (My Child); and costly donating behavior. Within time points we will test how these prosocial skills relate to both internalizing (SDQ subscales emotional problems + peer problems) and externalizing (SDQ subscale conduct problems + hyperactivity) problem behavior. The evidence on the relation between behavior problems and the three measures of prosocial skills will be aggregated by means of Bayesian evidence synthesis (Kuiper et al., 2013; Zondervan et al., 2019). This encompasses that we will use a set of competing informative hypotheses (Hoijtink, 2012), and evaluate which hypothesis receives most support by the data.

oer_title: Science beliefs, political ideology, and cognitive sophistication
oer_summary: A formatted word document of this preregistration is attached. The purpose of this study is to examine the extent to which people believe specific science topics and science facts (used in Studies 1 and 2) are politically divisive. Information from this study will be used to evaluate and reorganize the results that are already reported in Studies 1 and 2. The original goal of this set of studies was to generate a fairly comprehensive set of scientific issues in order to test several theoretically derived predictions. These predictions concerns tests of motivated reasoning and the politicization of science beliefs, but they also concern the extent to which science knowledge is a predictor of a range of science beliefs. Thus, political disagreement is not relevant to every analysis in this set of studies. Therefore, we outline a set of procedures below determining how we will use the information obtained in this test. Participants Participants (N = 200) are recruited from Lucid. Method Subjects are asked to consider 17 statements (e.g. "Global warming is at least partly caused by human activity and is a serious problem for the environment.") and 12 science facts (e.g. "Electrons are smaller than atoms") and are asked: "Do you think this is something that Democrats and Republicans are likely to disagree on?" Options are Yes or No. All items are presented in randomized order. Analysis All items are analyzed individually: The percentage of 'Yes' responses (e.g. indicating the belief that Democrats and Republicans would disagree) for each statement is calculated. The percentage of 'Yes' responses for each science fact is also calculated. Analysis script is attached. Data will be interpreted in percentages, only. There is no exclusion criteria; missing data will be treated as follows: If a subject is missing data on an item, they will be excluded from that calculation but will be included in other analyses for which they have data. Results Science statements with 50% agreement or greater will be considered politically divisive for the purposes of this study. We choose a 50% cutoff so that we can include a range of items that are politically divisive to a greater and lesser extent. That is, we don't want a set of only highly divisive items, but we want to identify meaningful disagreement. However, we do want to remove items for which there is unlikely to be any level of political disagreement (i.e. where agreement is less than 50%) from relevant analyses. No non-divisive items will be removed from analyses comparing the predictive power of ideology and deficit models. This includes tests of Fisher's r-to-z, and regression analyses using the composite liberal and conservative pro-science scales. Non-divisive items will be identified in all analyses using individual items, but the analyses as currently reported will remain the same. This includes the individual items correlations and the tests of political X cognitive sophistication interactions for each individual item. The 12 science facts are included here for comparative purposes only; we will not change any analyses or calculations based on whether or not people think these items are divisive.

oer_title: The Crowd(s) Within
oer_summary: Research question and hypothesis: The average of two estimates from the same person has been shown to be more accurate than each estimate on its own. Here, we investigate how taking a different perspective when making the second estimate (specifically, the perspective of a friend who often agrees with us, or a friend who often disagrees with us), impacts the benefit of averaging. We expect that the benefit of averaging, calculated by subtracting the mean squared error (MSE) of the average of two estimates, from the MSE of the first estimate, will depend on the conditions (i.e., the type of instructions people get on how to make the second estimate), and on the type of question that is asked. Specifically, for questions where the true answer is in the range from 0% to 9% or 91% to 100% (the extreme range questions - see below at the ‘dependent variables’ section), we expect that averaging the first and second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend people often disagree with, lowers the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This decrease in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger as compared to the condition in which people are instructed to make a second guess themselves (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008), or the condition where the second estimate is made from the perspective of a friend people often agree with. For all other questions (the middle range questions - see below at the ‘dependent variables’ section), we expect the reverse. That is, we expect that averaging the first and second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend people often disagree with, increases the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This increase in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger as compared to the condition in which the second estimate is a second guess people made themselves (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008), or the condition where the second estimate is made from the perspective of a friend people often agree with. Design: The study will have a 3 (Perspective taken in the second estimate: Self vs. Agreeing Friend vs. Disagreeing Friend) x 2 (Question Answers: Middle Range vs. Extreme range) mixed subject design. Perspective will be a between-, while Question Answers will be a within-subject factor. In all three between-subject conditions, participants will be instructed to try and answer 12 questions whose answer is always some percentage, ranging from 0% to 100%. Half of the questions will have answers that are in the extreme range. The other half will have answers that are in the middle range. The instructions about the second estimate will depend on the condition (see below). In all three conditions, participants will not be told at the beginning that they will have to make a second estimate. Manipulations: In the self perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be told to make a second guess. The same instructions will be used as in Vul and Pasher (2008) and Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, and Vanpaemel (2014). Specifically, the instruction will be: “We will now ask you to provide a second guess at the answer to each of the twelve questions you were asked in the first session. These answers should not be the same as your previous answers: these should reflect your ‘second guess’.” In the agreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very similar to yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself agreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these eight questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” In the disagreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very different from yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself disagreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these eight questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” Dependent variable(s): Participants will be asked to estimate the correct answer of 12 questions whose answer is always a percentage. They will be able to indicate their answer using a slider that ranges from 0% to 100%. As the middle range, we will consider the following questions: 1. What percent of the world’s airports are in the United States? (answer: 32.3%) 2. What percent of the world’s population lives in China, India, and the European Union? (answer: 43.2%) 3. What percent of the world’s countries have a higher fertility rate than the United States? (answer: 57.7%) 4. What percent of the world’s telephone lines are in China, USA, and the European Union? (answer: 53.3%) 5. Saudi Arabia consumes what percentage of the oil it produces? (answer: 32.5%) 6. What percentage of the world’s countries have a higher life expectancy than the United States? (answer: 19.6%) As the extreme range, we will consider the following questions: 1. The area of the USA is what percent of the area of the Pacific Ocean? (answer: 6.3%) 2. What percent of the world’s roads are in India? (answer: 7.3%) 3. What percent of China’s population identifies as Christian? (answer: 5.1%) 4. What percent of the US population is younger than 80? (answer: 96%) 5. What percent of the United Kingdom are internet users? (answer: 94.8%) 6. What percent of the US population owns a cellphone? (answer: 95%) Participants’ responses will be converted to mean squared errors. Data collection procedure: Data will be collected using the mTurk platform. Participants will be paid a fixed amount for their participation which will be limited to individuals from the United States? Analyses: In order to calculate the benefit of averaging, we will subtract the MSE of the average of two estimates from the MSE of the first estimate (rendering a difference score). The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first- and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). To test within each respective condition whether the average of the two estimates is more or less accurate than the first estimate (i.e., the within crowd effect), we will use dependent samples t-tests (two-sided). In order to compare the benefit of averaging between the different perspective conditions (i.e., comparing whether the difference score of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate is different per condition), we will use independent samples t-tests (two-sided). Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. For the attention check, participants have to read the full instructions of the question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any question. Sample size: As our main hypothesis concerns comparing the difference scores of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate across conditions, we will aim to recruit 290 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size was determined by performing a power analysis in G*Power to detect an effect of Cohen’s d = .30, with 95% power, and an alpha of .05. This means we plan to collect 900 participants in total to counteract a potential 2% exclusion rate. We use an effect size of .30 as a previous study we conducted obtained this as the lowest effect size when comparing the benefit of averaging between conditions. We opted to highly power our study to detect this effect, all the while having 80% power or more to detect an effect as low as Cohen’s d = .24. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 900 participants in total have taken the study on mTurk. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the mTurk platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.
